title: Wendell and the Parish
premise: When insurance investigator Wren Coldharbour receives a confession letter for a death ruled accidental—postmarked the day after the funeral of parish benefactor Edmund Vasse—she returns to the decaying village of Wendell, where she spent one invisible childhood summer. Using her photographic memory of the original case file, Wren realizes the killer is someone with access to every document, every statement, every lie: the investigation itself has been curated as an alibi. As the statute of limitations deadline looms, Wren discovers the confession was bait, designed to draw her back and make her the file's final entry. In the end she turns the killer's obsession with documentation against them, forcing a recorded confession in the flooded crypt beneath the parish church—and chooses to stay in Wendell, claiming the inheritance of belonging she never believed was hers.
about_author: Elodie Thackeray is the pen name of a former rural claims adjuster who spent a decade reading other people's disasters on paper. She writes mysteries about paper trails, small parishes, and the people history forgets to index.

chapters.title: Postmarked the Day After
chapters.summary: Wren Coldharbour, at her desk in London, receives a handwritten confession to the drowning of Edmund Vasse—dated before his death, postmarked after his funeral. Her photographic memory flags an impossibility in the postmark. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: the thrill of an unclosable case curdling into dread.

chapters.title: The File That Remembers
chapters.summary: Wren pulls the archived Vasse file from memory and finds eleven pages missing—pages only someone inside the claims office could have removed. She requests leave and takes the case off-book. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: quiet defiance; she breaks her own rule about cases she can't close.

chapters.title: Return to Wendell
chapters.summary: Wren arrives in the rain-soaked village, unrecognized by most but remembered by the innkeeper, Mrs. Tallow, who fed her the summer she was twelve. The parish church bell tolls wrong—one hour late. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: the ache of returning somewhere that half-remembers you.

chapters.title: A Summer She Buried
chapters.summary: Flashback woven through present: twelve-year-old Wren, fostered for a season, watched Edmund Vasse from the churchyard and memorized everything. Present-day Wren visits his grave and finds fresh flowers arranged in an insurer's knot—a signal meant for her. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: grief for the child she was.

chapters.title: The Benefactor's Ledger
chapters.summary: In the parish office, Wren meets Reverend Ansel Croft and discovers Vasse funded half the village through a private ledger—debts, favors, silences. Everyone had motive; everyone had a price. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: disillusionment as charity reveals itself as control.

chapters.title: The Handwriting Problem
chapters.summary: Wren compares the confession letter to Vasse's known correspondence: it's written in his hand—but Vasse was left-handed, and the letter shows right-slant pressure. A forgery by someone who studied him closely. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: cold excitement; the trap has edges now.

chapters.title: Eleven Missing Pages
chapters.summary: Wren reconstructs the missing file pages from memory and realizes they documented the original 'accident' scene—including a witness statement from someone officially listed as absent that day. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: vertigo as the official record proves itself a fiction.

chapters.title: Mrs. Tallow's Silence
chapters.summary: The innkeeper admits she saw something the night Vasse died but was paid to forget—by the same handwriting that signed Wren's childhood lodging voucher. Someone has been managing Wren's life too. POV: alternating Wren/Mrs. Tallow. Emotional beat: betrayal; even her past was edited.

chapters.title: The Curator
chapters.summary: Wren names her adversary privately: not a murderer but a curator, someone maintaining the story of Wendell like an archive. She finds her own childhood records altered—the summer she spent here officially never happened. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: terror of being erased.

chapters.title: Ansel Knows the File
chapters.summary: Reverend Croft quotes the missing pages verbatim over tea—then catches himself. He has read documents that no longer exist. Wren says nothing, but he knows she knows. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: cat-and-mouse tension beneath civility.

chapters.title: The Second Letter
chapters.summary: A second letter arrives, addressed to Wren by her childhood nickname that appears in no surviving record: 'You were always my best annotation.' The statute clock becomes explicit—nineteen days remain. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: hunted; the case has turned personal.

chapters.title: What the Bell Saw
chapters.summary: Investigating the late-tolling bell, Wren learns the church clock was tampered with the night Vasse died—an hour stolen to break an alibi or build one. The tower holds a scratched message: her own initials. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: claustrophobic revelation high above the village.

chapters.title: The Drowned Crypt
chapters.summary: Beneath the church, a partially flooded crypt holds Vasse's true archive: originals of every forged document, including Wren's erased records. The water rises with the tide; whoever built this collection expected a final visitor. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: awe and menace in the dark.

chapters.title: Confession as Bait
chapters.summary: Wren works out the design: the confession letter was written to lure an investigator with her exact skills back to Wendell, so the curator could close the last open file—hers. She decides to let herself be caught. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: resolve; turning prey into trap-setter.

chapters.title: Nineteen Becomes Nine
chapters.summary: A near-miss: Wren's room is searched, her reconstructed pages photographed. She stages a false version to feed the curator misinformation about what she knows. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: paranoia sharpened into discipline.

chapters.title: The Village Chooses
chapters.summary: Wren shares fragments of truth with key villagers—Tallow, the sexton, the publican—and finds they already suspected but chose comfort over knowledge. Some refuse to help; three quietly agree. POV: multiple villagers then Wren. Emotional beat: the cost and grace of collective complicity breaking.

chapters.title: Croft's Sermon
chapters.summary: Reverend Croft preaches on inheritance and debt, looking at Wren throughout. Afterward he offers her Vasse's seat as parish benefactor—an inheritance in exchange for silence. She declines. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: temptation made explicit and refused.

chapters.title: The Annotation Speaks
chapters.summary: Following the curator's logic, Wren plants a final 'page'—a fabricated witness statement—in the parish office and watches who retrieves it. It's not Croft. It's the archivist, Miss Verity Latch, the woman who catalogued Wren's childhood summer. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: shock reorganized instantly into strategy.

chapters.title: Why You Were Chosen
chapters.summary: Confronted in the crypt, Latch confesses her philosophy: Vasse corrupted the parish with money, so she corrupted the record to hold power over power—editing Wendell until only she knew its true text. She killed him when he tried to reclaim his papers. POV: Latch, then Wren. Emotional beat: horror at power's purest form—narrative control.

chapters.title: The Rising Water
chapters.summary: Latch seals the crypt as the tide floods in, intending Wren to become the archive's final, drowned entry. Wren uses her perfect memory to recite Latch's crimes aloud while the three allies—warned by the false page's timing—break the seal above. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: survival by testimony; memory as weapon.

chapters.title: Recorded in Full
chapters.summary: With the confession witnessed and recorded, Latch collapses into the identity of a footnote. The statute expires hours later, but the living witnesses stand outside any file now. Wren hands the true archive to the village, not the authorities. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: justice imperfect but shared.

chapters.title: The Hour the Bell Keeps
chapters.summary: Spring comes to Wendell. Wren repairs the church clock herself, sets the bell right, and signs a lease on the cottage she once stayed in as a child—her first honest entry in the parish record. Belonging, she writes, is the only inheritance worth keeping. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: quiet arrival home.
